title: Jeremiah 23:33–40
context: The LORD forbids the phrase rendered “the message from the LORD” (23:33–40). The Hebrew word behind “message” can mean both an oracle and a burden, something carried, and many interpreters see a play on that double sense: those who glibly ask for the LORD’s message are answered, “I will cast you off” (23:33). The people are told instead to ask plainly, “What has the LORD answered?” (23:35, 37). The exact reasons for the prohibition are not fully spelled out, and explanations are held with caution.

verses.text: “When this people, or the prophet, or a priest, asks you, saying, ‘What is the message from the LORD?’ Then you shall tell them, ‘ “What message? I will cast you off,” says the LORD.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah how to answer when asked, “What is the message from the LORD?” Arminian readers see the people’s question met with the reply, “I will cast you off,” a sharp turn of their own words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a play on the word rendered “message,” which can also mean a burden. Readers in this tradition commonly take the answer as turning a casual request for an oracle into a word of judgment.

verses.text: As for the prophet, the priest, and the people, who say, ‘The message from the LORD,’ I will even punish that man and his household.
verses.arminianNotes: “As for the prophet, the priest, and the people, who say, ‘The message from the LORD,’ I will even punish that man and his household.” Arminian readers see the phrase misused as a mere slogan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a familiar religious phrase used carelessly. The text does not spell out every reason for the prohibition, and readers in this tradition hold explanations of it with some caution.

verses.text: You will say everyone to his neighbor, and everyone to his brother, ‘What has the LORD answered?’ and, ‘What has the LORD said?’
verses.arminianNotes: “You will say everyone to his neighbor, and everyone to his brother, ‘What has the LORD answered?’ and, ‘What has the LORD said?’” Arminian readers see plainer, humbler questions commended.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the people directed to ask simply what the LORD has said. Readers in this tradition see the contrast between seeking God’s actual word and repeating a loaded phrase.

verses.text: You will mention the message from the LORD no more, for every man’s own word has become his message; for you have perverted the words of the living God, of the LORD of Armies, our God.
verses.arminianNotes: “You will mention the message from the LORD no more, for every man’s own word has become his message.” Arminian readers see the phrase emptied by people who put their own words in God’s mouth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the perversion of “the words of the living God.” Readers in this tradition hear the verse as exposing how religious language can become cover for human opinion.

verses.text: You will say to the prophet, ‘What has the LORD answered you?’ and, ‘What has the LORD spoken?’
verses.arminianNotes: “You will say to the prophet, ‘What has the LORD answered you?’ and, ‘What has the LORD spoken?’” Arminian readers see the right way to approach a prophet, seeking God’s word rather than a slogan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a return to the plain question that seeks God’s word. Readers in this tradition note the repetition of 23:35, reinforcing the contrast with the forbidden phrase.

verses.text: Although you say, ‘The message from the LORD,’ therefore the LORD says: ‘Because you say this word, “The message from the LORD,” and I have sent to you, telling you not to say, “The message from the LORD,”
verses.arminianNotes: “Because you say this word, ‘The message from the LORD,’ and I have sent to you, telling you not to say, ‘The message from the LORD,’” Arminian readers see persistent refusal of a clear command.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the people’s continued disobedience after warning. Readers in this tradition note that the judgment that follows is tied to stubborn rejection of what God has plainly said.

verses.text: therefore behold, I will utterly forget you, and I will cast you off with the city that I gave to you and to your fathers, away from my presence.
verses.arminianNotes: “… therefore behold, I will utterly forget you, and I will cast you off with the city that I gave to you and to your fathers.” Arminian readers see the gravity of rejecting God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see covenant judgment in the casting off of the city. Readers in this tradition read the verse alongside the hope of return in 23:3–8 and 24:6–7, holding judgment and promise together.

verses.text: I will bring an everlasting reproach on you, and a perpetual shame, which will not be forgotten.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will bring an everlasting reproach on you, and a perpetual shame, which will not be forgotten.” Arminian readers see the lasting consequence of the generation’s rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a severe and lasting judgment. Readers in this tradition note that the same book promises restoration, and they do not read this verse as cancelling God’s wider covenant purpose.
